title: Oeta – 1956
lede: Victor Vasarely’s screenprint after a 1956 composition: a black and white grid of squares that shears and twists, between large black and white rhombs on a grey ground.
summary: A black-square grid that distorts into rhombs, with large tilted black and white blocks on grey. Victor Vasarely, screenprint, 1959.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, CIRC.682-1965 (1267 × 1600 px), with a colour bar at the side, in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Vasarely’s black and white period in print: a regular grid of squares that bends into rhombs to suggest folding and depth.

context: The V&A describes a colour screenprint on paper, 55.5 × 36.8 cm, made in France in 1959, acquired in 1965. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O71746/).

The V&A calls Vasarely (1908–1997) one of the leading artists of the movement later named Op art, whose aim was to make a static surface seem to move, and notes his use of cheap screenprinting for multiples. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O71746/).
observed: A mid-grey rectangle sits on a white sheet. On it, a wide band holds a grid of black squares on white.
In parts of the grid the squares rotate or shear into rhombs, so the band seems to fold and ripple.
Large black squares and black-and-white rhombs, tilted at different angles, sit above and below the grid.
Only black, white, and one grey appear.
interpretation: Oeta shows the checkerboard as a surface under stress: a few units change shape, and the whole plane seems to bend.
The grey ground is the one step in the value scale that the style record allows.
borrow: Take a strict grid of black squares and shear a few rows or cells into rhombs to suggest a fold.
Use one mid-grey as a ground to separate a black and white pattern from a white page.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Vasarely died in 1997, so the work is in copyright until 2067 in France.
